kit.name: ELEGOO UNO R3 Super Starter Kit

identity.canonical_name: brushed DC motor with fan blade (130-size)
identity.manufacturer: unbranded / generic (ELEGOO does not name a motor manufacturer for this part)
identity.manufacturer_part_number: none published by ELEGOO; commonly called a "130-size" brushed DC motor, comparable to Adafruit PID 711 and Handson Technology FAM1072
generic_equivalents: Handson Technology 130 Brushed High Speed Mini DC Motor (SKU FAM1072)
identity.package: 130-size can motor with two solder-tab or bare-wire leads

function.one_sentence_plain_english: A small electric motor that spins a plastic fan blade the moment it gets power.
function.what_it_is_used_for: Teaches how to drive a simple DC motor, here used as a fan, through a motor driver chip instead of wiring it straight to a microcontroller pin.
function.how_it_works_briefly: Current flowing through the internal coil, working against the motor's permanent magnets, makes the shaft spin. Swapping which of the two leads is positive reverses the spin direction. The plastic fan blade is press-fit onto the output shaft.

pinout.name: Terminal A
pinout.notes: either lead can be wired to positive

pinout.name: Terminal B
pinout.notes: swapping the two leads reverses spin direction

pins.pin_1_identification: No fixed positive terminal on this class of motor. Either metal tab/lead can be wired as positive; swapping the two just reverses the spin direction rather than causing damage.

electrical.operating_voltage: 3-6V DC (as printed on the ELEGOO kit tutorial for this part)
electrical.absolute_max_voltage: not published by ELEGOO for this exact unit; generic 130-size motors are not usually run above about 9V
electrical.typical_current: roughly 70-250 mA at rated voltage, no-load to lightly loaded (typical for this motor class, per the Adafruit PID 711 listing)
electrical.max_current: roughly 500 mA to 1 A stall current (typical for this motor class, per Adafruit PID 711 and Handson Technology FAM1072 listings; varies by manufacturer)
electrical.logic_level: none, this is a mechanical load, not a logic device

key_specs.no_load_speed_rpm: roughly 9,000-26,000 RPM depending on supply voltage and the specific unit (per Adafruit PID 711 and Handson Technology FAM1072 listings)
key_specs.shaft: about 2mm round shaft; the fan blade press-fits directly onto it

visual_identification.shape_and_size: Small cylindrical metal can, roughly 20-28mm long and about 20mm in diameter, with a multi-blade plastic fan pressed onto a thin metal shaft at one end.
visual_identification.color_and_markings: Plain silver or grey metal case with no printed text or brand markings.
visual_identification.printed_text_to_look_for: Usually none. Occasionally a tiny voltage-rating sticker on the can, but ELEGOO's unit typically ships unmarked.
easily_confused_with: 28BYJ-48 stepper motor (larger, blue plastic body with a 5-wire cable, not a bare metal can)
SG90 servo motor (has a 3-wire cable and a gearbox housing, not a bare motor can)

example_connections.uno_pin: L293D output pin (e.g. 1Y), never directly to an UNO pin
L293D output pin (e.g. 2Y), never directly to an UNO pin

required_extra_parts: Power Supply Module (recommended over powering the motor from the UNO's own 5V pin)
wiring_to_uno.arduino_library: none required; driven with plain digitalWrite()/analogWrite() through the L293D

hazards: Never wire the motor directly to a digital pin; switching it off induces a voltage spike that can damage the UNO
A spinning fan blade can pinch skin or catch loose hair or wires at high RPM
handling_notes: Always drive it through a motor driver IC (L293D) or a transistor with a flyback diode, never straight from a microcontroller pin
Keep fingers and wires clear of the blade while powered
common_mistakes: Wiring the motor directly to an UNO pin instead of through the L293D
Expecting a fixed polarity; if the fan spins the 'wrong' way, just swap the two leads

symptoms_and_causes.symptom: Motor does not spin at all
symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: No power reaching the L293D output, or its enable pin is left low
symptoms_and_causes.check: Measure DC voltage across the motor terminals with a multimeter while the sketch is running

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: The two motor leads are swapped relative to what the sketch expects
symptoms_and_causes.check: Swap the two wires at the L293D output connections

symptoms_and_causes.likely_cause: Insufficient supply voltage/current from the Power Supply Module, or the blade is physically obstructed
symptoms_and_causes.check: Check the Power Supply Module's output jumper setting and confirm nothing is blocking the fan blade

troubleshooting.how_to_test_with_a_multimeter: With power off, set the multimeter to resistance mode and touch a probe to each terminal; a healthy motor reads a low, stable resistance of a few ohms. With power on and the motor commanded on, switch to DC voltage mode across the terminals to confirm the driver is actually delivering voltage.
